Here's what you owe

lines.text: Card number stolen? The law says you owe exactly this much.
lines.say: Card number stolen? The law says you owe exactly this much.

lines.text: $0. Under federal law, if only the number is stolen, not the card, you're not liable.
lines.say: Zero dollars. Under federal law, if only the number is stolen, not the card itself, you're not on the hook.

lines.text: And it's surging: 597,770 credit card fraud reports to the FTC in 2025, up 33% from 2024.
lines.say: And it's surging. The F T C got about five hundred ninety-eight thousand credit card fraud reports in twenty twenty-five, up thirty-three percent from twenty twenty-four.

lines.text: Say a thief spends $1,200 on your number. Your share on a credit card: $0.
lines.say: Say a thief spends twelve hundred dollars on your number. Your share on a credit card is zero.

lines.text: Debit cards are different. Report a lost card after 2 business days, and you could lose up to $500.
lines.say: Debit cards are different. Report a lost card after two business days, and you could lose up to five hundred dollars.

lines.text: Don't report within 60 days of your statement, and new withdrawals may not be covered at all.
lines.say: Don't report within sixty days of your statement, and new withdrawals may not be covered at all.

lines.text: So call your card issuer fast, then dispute in writing within 60 days of the first statement that shows the charge.

post.title: Someone stole your credit card number. Here's what you owe.
post.ig:
Card number stolen? Under federal law, you owe $0.
Your max liability for unauthorized credit card use is $50, and $0 if only the number was stolen, not the card.
Debit is different: report a lost card after 2 business days and you could lose up to $500; new withdrawals after 60+ days past your statement may not be covered at all.
The FTC got 597,770 credit card fraud reports in 2025, up 33% from 2024.
Sources: FTC; CFPB (Regulation Z, Regulation E).
News and education, not financial advice.
